newsitem.title: GEORGIA: Georgia slams Russia on fleet, Abkhaz row rumbles.
newsitem.headline: Georgia slams Russia on fleet, Abkhaz row rumbles.

text.p: Georgian President Eduard Shevadnadze criticised Russia on Monday for what he said was its "heartless" refusal to allow his country a share of the former Soviet Black Sea fleet.

His comments coincide with the leader of Georgia's breakaway Abkazia region holding talks in Moscow. He renewed warnings that Georgian threats to push Russian peacekeepers out of a buffer zone could rekindle a war that killed 10,000 people in 1992-93.

Russia and Ukraine resolved their five-year dispute over the Black Sea fleet last month, leaving three months to agree on how divide up ships and property. The fleet's main base is in what is now the Ukrainian city of Sevastopol.

Kremlin officials said Georgian claims to a share of it were "groundless". The mountainous country of about six million has about 350 km (200 miles) of Black Sea coast, much of which is occupied by the secessionist Abkhaz forces in the northwest.

"Some Russian bureaucrats and state officials have reacted very heartlessly and even cynically to our requests to hand over to us a share of the former Soviet Black Sea fleet," Shevardnadze said in his weekly radio address.
Shevardnadze, the former Soviet foreign minister, said the issue threatened overall Georgian-Russian relations.
"Such an attitude makes it difficult to develop a strategic partnership between Georgia and Russia," he said.
The dispute over the fleet emerged as Russia's peacekeeping mission in Georgia's secessionist-minded province of Abkhazia faced increasing criticism by Tbilisi.

Georgia wants the withdrawal of the 2,500-strong force, stationed in a buffer zone along the de-facto Abkhaz-Georgian border, after August 1 if Moscow does not agree to patrol more of Abkhazia and help resettle Georgian refugees.
A Kremlin spokesman last week called that "blackmail".

Georgian Interior Minister Kakha Targamadze accused members of the force on Sunday of involvement in "unlawful arrests, savage murders, and punitive operations" against civilians living in the security zone since they began patrols in 1994.
Shevardnadze said that showed the need to "analyse and fully think through the work of the peacekeepers and their mission".
Targamadze said that 183 Georgian complaints to Russian military prosecutors had brought no action.
Abkhaz leader Vladislav Ardzinba met the head of Russian President Boris Yeltsin's administration, the Russian foreign and defence ministers and other officials in Moscow.
He warned against withdrawing the troops.
"I wouldn't say that it is a hundred percent certain that it would lead to a renewal of hostilities, but naturally the threat of hostilities would grow," Ardzinba told Ekho Moskvy radio.

The Kremlin issued a statement after the talks saying Moscow "stressed the pressing need for the soonest possible signing by the parties to the confict of a document which would put an end to the state of war".
Moscow wants Georgia and Abkhazia to agree to U.N.-sponsored peace talks and is prepared guarantee any peace settlement
The two sides, however, seem far apart, with Georgia unwilling to grant Abkhazia the degree of autonomy it wants.
Abkhazia, a lush subtropical Black Sea region, has enjoyed de facto independence since 1993 when its fighters routed Georgian forces. But no country has recognised its sovereignty.
Shevardnadze said last month it would be "suicide" for the Abkhaz to take on the rebuilt Georgian armed forces.
